doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Mingus's singing of parts and Sarah's rehearsals
summary: Mingus sang parts to Knepper and Hanna and shifted time with Danny Richmond; Sarah loved rehearsal and made him write charts for Reno.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players

blocks.x: Was there a lot of singing of parts to you?
And you had to like get them that way?

Yes. Mingus would sing out parts. He’d sing out the things he’d want. It wasn’t until later that he started to work with Sy Johnson. He was working with Jimmy Knepper first. And Jimmy Knepper used to help him to write out his parts. Then later when he got older and he couldn’t really write anymore, he started to get that disease, he got Sy Johnson to help him. But when Knepper was working with him he’d sing thing to Knepper and Knepper would write them down and then they’d put it together. And he used to do that to me if he wanted a certain chord. He’d sing a certain thing, and try to play the bass note, and then I would give him the chord and tell him what it was. Because he didn’t know. As great as he was, sometimes he didn’t know the chord. Mingus had played with Art Tatum and played with Duke Ellington, had played with a great many pianists. But the actual harmony he didn’t always know. And we’d sit down and talk a lot about academic harmony. What he did know was how to play the bass. He was a phenomenal bass player. You can’t take anything away from Mingus in terms of that bass. But he didn’t have much stamina for steady, steady, steady tempo. And I think that’s one of the reasons why he did something new in jazz, giving jazz this shift of rhythm and shift of time, starting out with one kind of time and then, without a conductor, changing it suddenly. And it was a good thing that he had Danny Richmond with him for so long because Danny was with him like they were like on water skis going together, shift the time just like that. But with Sarah there was a different situation. She loved to rehearse. She didn’t like to sing at the rehearsals but she loved to rehearse. Wherever we played, when we got there we usually rehearsed three or four hours. And there would be some new tunes, and she would give me ideas as to how to set up the arrangement. The scary time that I had with Sarah was when we played Harrah’s in Reno, Nevada. This was like the first gig where we had a band. And she didn’t tell me that I’m supposed to write out the arrangements for the band. So when we get there, suddenly the guys said, “Where are the arrangements, where are the parts?” I had to sit up like the whole weekend and write arrangements. This was the kind of taskmaster she was. She said, “Look it’s your gig, you’re my musical director, it’s your gig, get my charts.”
